papers.title: Automated Sleep Staging Performance Across Two Experimental Sleep Manipulation Protocols in Adolescents.
papers.abstract: Automated sleep staging algorithms improve the scalability of polysomnography analysis in adolescent research but are primarily validated in undisturbed, single-night sleep recordings. It remains unclear whether these algorithms maintain performance when sleep architecture is experimentally manipulated. This study evaluated the validity of two popular automated sleep staging approaches across two distinct sleep manipulation paradigms in adolescents: a sleep restriction protocol (N=43, mean age [SD]=13.37[1.06] years; four nights including two sleep extension [10hr] and two restriction [4hr] nights) and a slow-wave sleep deprivation (SWSD) protocol (N=18, mean age [SD]=17.17[1.79] years; baseline, SWSD, and recovery nights). Automated sleep staging was performed using the POPulation-level Sleep Stager (POPS), the Yet Another Spindle Algorithm (YASA), and combined POPS+YASA. Manual polysomnography scoring by experienced sleep technicians served as the reference standard. Agreement was assessed using Cohen's κ, and stage-specific performance was evaluated using F1 scores and confusion matrices. Mixed-effects models tested differences in overall and stage-specific agreement across nights. All staging approaches demonstrated moderate-to-substantial agreement with manual scoring across manipulated sleep conditions (κ range=0.53-0.76). In the sleep restriction study, agreement was lower in restricted versus extended sleep (P<0.05), and agreement declined across restriction nights, with poorer Wake, N1, and N2 classification, while N3 remained preserved. In the SWSD study, overall agreement was lower on the SWSD night, with poorer N3 classification while other stages were preserved. Automated sleep staging performance may be less consistent in adolescents when sleep is curtailed or fragmented; future studies should develop and validate these algorithms under multiple sleep conditions.

papers.title: Comprehensive benchmarking of EEG biomarkers for Parkinson's disease: robustness, reliability, and clinical discriminability across multiple datasets.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a high-temporal-resolution, noninvasive window into some of the abnormalities underlying Parkinson's disease (PD), yet reported electrophysiological biomarkers vary widely across studies due to differences in preprocessing, feature extraction, and analytical pipelines. Here we provide the first comprehensive, multi-dataset benchmarking of 16 EEG-derived biomarkers, including phase-amplitude coupling, beta burst metrics, aperiodic components, complexity measures, and beta waveform features, to evaluate their robustness, reliability, and clinical discriminability. Using three independent resting-state EEG datasets, with two preprocessing conditions evaluated for one dataset, we assessed the effects of preprocessing, window length, within-session variability, channel aggregation strategies, and clinical group differences (healthy controls vs. PD OFF-medication, healthy controls vs. PD ON-medication, and PD OFF- vs. ON-medication). Cross-dataset reproducibility of group-level effects was additionally evaluated using effect-size pattern similarity, biomarker rank concordance, effect-direction consistency, and random-effects meta-analysis. Aperiodic features, entropy and complexity measures, and fractal metrics demonstrated high methodological robustness across preprocessing methods, window lengths, and aggregation strategies, and several showed disease- and medication-related effects across datasets, although effect magnitude and statistical significance varied across datasets and analytical conditions. In contrast, oscillatory biomarkers, including beta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, burst-derived metrics, and waveform-asymmetry features, showed substantial variability across methodological choices and lower within-session consistency. However, this methodological sensitivity should not necessarily be interpreted as lower biological relevance, as these measures may capture more transient or state-dependent physiological dynamics. Fully-denoised data improved group-level separability, for several biomarkers in Dataset 1. Together, these findings identify several biomarkers with comparatively strong methodological robustness for further biological and clinical validation and highlight methodological factors that contribute to inconsistencies in the PD literature. This benchmarking framework provides practical guidance for standardizing biomarker analysis while emphasizing that methodological robustness, biological sensitivity, and clinical utility represent distinct dimensions of biomarker performance.

papers.title: Coverage collapse and deceptive calibration in EEG fatigue monitoring: a cross-dataset audit under within-session and cross-subject shift.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography-based driver fatigue monitors are judged almost entirely on accuracy, yet a safety monitor is useful only if its stated confidence can be trusted when it is wrong. We audit whether it survives drift within a recording and transfer to a new person.Approach. Five model families, from a dense network to a gradient-boosted tree ensemble, run on three public corpora differing in channels, label instrument and elicitation. Calibration is measured pooled, per recording and per class, beside proper scoring rules. Seven conformal recalibration strategies are compared under one protocol, and we derive a ceiling on the coverage attainable by any rule thresholding a fixed calibration set.Main results. Pooled calibration error falls as accuracy falls, so the headline reliability metric improves as the model degrades. Aggregated per recording, the same predictions reverse it, exceeding the pooled estimate in all fifteen session-time bins of both continuously annotated corpora (sign test, p = 3.1 × 10⁻⁵); on the fatigued class the concealed error reaches 4.9 times the pooled value. Under transfer, class-balanced calibration error rises by 0.107 to 0.254 in all fifteen model-corpus cells, where coverage falls below its 0.90 target, to 0.533 at worst, with empty prediction sets in four. The ceiling held on all 32 subject streams and bound 20 below target, separating recoverable methods in advance. Rolling re-estimation under a finite-sample correction cleared it on 19 of those 20, held 0.886 to 0.909 in every cell, and cut between-subject coverage variability from 0.205 to 0.026 at constant update cost.Significance. Pooled calibration error and marginal coverage can both look healthy while a monitor is least reliable in the states that should raise an alarm. Three cheap diagnostics separate a calibrated monitor from one averaging failures of opposite sign, and one that covers from one that abstains.

papers.title: Sleep-like slow waves in wakefulness index post-stroke behavioural alterations.
papers.abstract: Increases in high-amplitude, low-frequency EEG oscillations during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep serve as markers of neuronal silencing, which disrupts functional connectivity and is associated with a loss of awareness and responsiveness. Cortical slowing likewise occurs during wakefulness, upon sleep deprivation, and accompanies performance deterioration. Recent work has revealed similar oscillations (termed 'sleep-like slow waves') following stroke in brain regions close or connected to a brain lesion, offering a plausible but untested mechanism for stroke-related behavioural impairment. Here, we simultaneously recorded EEG and behavioural performance while 30 unilateral stroke patients (12 left hemisphere, 18 right hemisphere) and 27 age-matched healthy adults completed a computerised perceptual decision-making task. Stroke patients had predominantly middle cerebral artery strokes (n=25), with a small subset of posterior cerebral artery (n=4), and anterior cerebral artery/middle cerebral artery (n=1) lesions. Sleep-like slow waves occurred more frequently in stroke patients relative to healthy controls, with limited spatial specificity when comparing patients with left and right lesion sites (more slow waves ipsilateral of the lesion). Furthermore, there was a significant correlation between slow wave occurrence and the accuracy and speed of perceptual reports in stroke patients, suggesting that variations in the occurrence of slow waves may contribute to cognitive heterogeneity post-stroke. As sleep-like slow waves predict deficits in perceptual decision-making following stroke, they represent a plausible mechanism of post-lesion functional network dysfunction extending beyond the damaged regions, thereby contributing to broader cognitive impairments.

papers.title: Detection of Spreading Depolarization with Noninvasive Electroencephalography.
papers.abstract: Spreading depolarizations (SDs) are waves of near-complete breakdown of the transmembrane ion gradients that underlie migraine aura and occur in patients with moderate-to-severe traumatic, ischemic or hemorrhagic brain injury. SDs are involved in primary and secondary brain injury. They are associated with poor neurological outcome and represent a modifiable therapeutic target. However, despite decades of investigation, SD detection still requires invasive subdural electrocorticography (ECoG) using an implanted subdural electrode strip, restricting monitoring to a small subset of neurosurgical patients. We developed WAVEFRONT, a noninvasive scalp electroencephalography (EEG) biomarker of SD based on spatiotemporal propagation characteristics of delta-band EEG activity. The biomarker was trained and validated using concurrent, multi-day scalp EEG and invasive subdural electrocorticography recordings from patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI), subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), or malignant hemispheric stroke (MHS) across three institutions. We assessed out-of-sample performance across institutions, diagnosis, and surgical approaches, as well as calibration, temporal synchrony, and spatial specificity relative to gold-standard SDs annotated on ECoG. Clinical utility was further evaluated in 607 patients comatose after cardiac arrest from the multicenter International Cardiac Arrest REsearch (I-CARE) consortium, a population in whom invasive monitoring is not performed. Outcome analyses excluded patients who died (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 5) because death may reflect decisions to withdraw life-sustaining treatment in addition to neurological injury. A total of 1,119 gold-standard SDs were annotated in 32 patients (TBI, n=17; SAH, n=12; MHS, n=3; range 0-187 SDs per patient). Across exhaustive cross-validation and institution-, diagnosis-, and surgical approach-based hold-out analyses, WAVEFRONT models trained on one set of patients consistently maintained high performance when evaluated in previously unseen out-of-group cohorts. At the optimal operating point, WAVEFRONT achieved a mean cross-validated true positive rate of 97.3±1% with a false positive rate of 6.0±0.5%, calculated over 2-min sliding windows with 30-s overlaps. The cumulative duration of WAVEFRONT detections within 30-hour windows strongly correlated with the number of SDs measured by invasive ECoG (R 2 =0.7411). Scalp-detected depressions were spatially consistent with the location of the invasive recording strip, and visual inspection demonstrated close temporal correspondence with invasive detections, including during SD clusters. External validation in the independent I-CARE cohort using WAVEFRONT trained on the invasive-monitoring cohort demonstrated significantly greater SD burden on day 3 of post-arrest EEG monitoring among patients with poor neurological outcome (CPC 3-4, n=29) than those with good outcome (CPC 1-2, n=225; p=0.007). Eight decades after Leão's description of SD in 1944, we propose and validate a noninvasive scalp EEG biomarker of SD. Consistent performance across institution-, diagnosis-, and surgical approach-based hold-out analyses, together with burden calibration, spatial specificity, and temporal synchrony with ECoG detections, supports the validity of the WAVEFRONT framework. The association of biomarker burden with neurologic outcome after cardiac arrest suggests that noninvasive monitoring may enable investigation of spreading depolarizations in populations where invasive monitoring is not feasible. Future studies should evaluate prospective performance, treatment responsiveness, and disease-specific associations of the SD biomarker with clinical outcome.

papers.title: Temporal Associations Between Physiological Sleep and Next-Day Pain Intensity in Individuals With Activity-Limiting Chronic Pain: A Multiple Night At-Home Ear-EEG Sleep-Monitoring Study.
papers.abstract: Chronic pain and sleep disturbances frequently co-occur. However, most prior research relies on self-report or actigraphy, which reflect behavioural aspects of sleep but provide only limited insight into the underlying sleep physiology. In this pre-registered prospective observational study (NCT06368531), we investigated within-person night-to-night variability in physiological sleep metrics and explored temporal associations between sleep metrics and next-day pain. Individuals with bothersome (n = 4) or high-impact (n = 15) chronic pain completed between 11 and 33 nights of at-home sleep monitoring using an ear-EEG device and rated morning pain intensity daily on a 0-10 numerical rating scale. This design enables assessment of real-world physiological sleep patterns alongside natural fluctuations in pain, offering a high-resolution view of sleep-pain dynamics beyond traditional diary or actigraphy-based methods. Substantial between-night variability was observed across multiple sleep metrics, such as sleep efficiency and sleep stage transitions (ICC values < 0.5), indicating that less than half of the total variance was attributable to differences between subjects, underscoring the importance of longitudinal within-person monitoring. Mixed-effects model analyses revealed that lower next-day pain intensity was associated with greater duration (β = -0.01, p = 0.005), higher percentage (β = -0.07, p = 0.001) and increased stability (β = -0.01, p = 0.013) of N3 sleep. In contrast, higher next-day pain was associated with increased N3 fragmentation (β = 0.01, p = 0.014) and a higher proportion of N1 sleep (β = 0.014, p = 0.007). Together, these findings provide objective physiological support for previously reported associations between sleep and pain, highlighting the value of longitudinal ear-EEG monitoring for capturing nightly sleep-pain dynamics. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06368531.

papers.title: Next generation Human Neocortical Neurosolver model with biophysically realistic somatic, dendritic and synaptic dynamics
papers.abstract: The Human Neocortical Neurosolver (HNN) is an open-source biophysical modeling tool for multiscale interpretation of human electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) signals. HNN's foundation is a pre-tuned canonical neocortical circuit model consisting of excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons in supra- (L2/3) and infragranular (L5) layers. This model was originally developed based on studies in rodent and non-human primate cortices when dynamics of human neurons were poorly characterized. Yet recent advances in recordings from human tissue now provide unprecedented detail to update the model. Here, we present a significantly updated model for use in the HNN software, with electrophysiological properties and synaptic connections tuned to human tissue. Beyond reproducing biologically realistic somatic dynamics, the pyramidal cells simulate dendritic calcium (Ca2+) spikes in the L5 extratelencephalic-projecting (ET) neurons, and shorter dendritic spikes in the L2/3 pyramidal neurons. We demonstrate how the updated circuitry and new features in the HNN software can be used to disentangle somatic, synaptic, and dendritic contributions to human E-/MEG signatures. The model is distributed with workflows to simulate event-related responses and oscillations, and tutorials demonstrating how membrane potentials, Ca2+ dynamics, and synaptic currents can be recorded and visualized. These enhancements allow extensive model validations based on in vitro and in vivo electrophysiology, voltage and Ca2+ imaging, and provide users with novel insights on the mechanisms underlying E-/MEG signals.

papers.title: Disrupted sleep-wake regulation in the MCI-Park mouse model of Parkinson's Disease
papers.abstract: Disrupted sleep has a profound adverse impact on lives of Parkinson's Disease (PD) patients and their caregivers. Sleep disturbances are exceedingly common in PD, with substantial heterogeneity in type, timing, and severity. Among the most common sleep-related symptoms reported by PD patients are insomnia, excessive daytime sleepiness, and sleep fragmentation, characterized by interruptions and decreased continuity of sleep. Alterations in brain wave activity, as measured on the electroencephalogram (EEG), also occur in PD, with changes in the pattern and relative contributions of different frequency bands of the EEG spectrum to overall EEG activity in different vigilance states consistently observed. The mechanisms underlying these PD-associated sleep-wake abnormalities are poorly understood, and they are ineffectively treated by conventional PD therapies. To help fill this gap in knowledge, a new progressive model of PD - the MCI-Park mouse- was studied. Near the transition to the parkinsonian state, these mice exhibited significantly altered sleep-wake regulation, including increased wakefulness, decreased non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, increased sleep fragmentation, reduced rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, and altered EEG activity patterns. These sleep-wake abnormalities mirror those identified in PD patients. Thus, this model may help elucidate the circuit mechanisms underlying sleep disruption in PD and identify targets for novel therapeutic approaches.

papers.title: Characterising cortical perturbation-recovery dynamics using TMSEEG: The Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox
papers.abstract: Objective: To adapt dynamical measures used in computational and experimental perturbation models to human transcranial magnetic stimulation and electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and determine whether analysis of the extended post-stimulation trajectory reveals additional features of the cortical response to long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI). Methods: Single pulse and paired pulse LICI TMS-EEG responses from the bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex were re-analysed in 16 healthy adults. At the stimulation site, 75 single-pulse and 75 paired-pulse trials were delivered; paired pulses comprised conditioning and test stimuli separated by 100 ms. Responses from 20 frontocentral EEG channels were analysed from 50-950 ms following TMS using the open source Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox. Perturbative Integration Latency Index (PILI) indexed cortical resilience via response energy and recovery, Autocorrelation Function Width (ACFW) captured temporal memory, and Lyapunov Exponent (LE) indicated the dynamical stability. Linear mixed-effects models examined temporal, spectral, and time-frequency effects from the measured metrics. Results: LICI altered the temporal evolution of the dynamical measures. PILI distinguished conditions in the earliest post-stimulation window before converging, whereas ACFW differences persisted across a broader early interval. LE showed weaker and less consistent discrimination. Spectral effects were most evident for ACFW, while time-frequency analyses revealed later, frequency-specific LICI effects for PILI and ACFW but not LE. Conclusions: The extended post-stimulation trajectory revealed LICI-related differences in cortical resilience and temporal memory with distinct temporal and spectral profiles, while effects on dynamical stability were less consistent. Significance: The Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox provides a reproducible framework for quantifying perturbation-recovery dynamics in TMS-EEG and demonstrates that the extended perturbational response contains information about LICI not captured by discrete early response measures.

ai.summary: The study adapted dynamical measures from computational perturbation models to TMS-EEG data and applied them to analyze cortical perturbation-recovery dynamics in 16 healthy adults during long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI). It found that LICI altered the temporal evolution of dynamical measures: Perturbative Integration Latency Index distinguished conditions in the earliest post-stimulation window, Autocorrelation Function Width differences persisted across a broader early interval, and Lyapunov Exponent showed weaker discrimination, demonstrating that extended post-stimulation trajectories reveal additional features of cortical resilience and temporal memory.

papers.title: EEG-based deep learning estimates preterm infants' cerebral age: Contribution of slow-wave and cross-frequency coupling.
papers.abstract: Reliably estimating cerebral maturation in preterm newborns is crucial for early identification of atypical neurodevelopment. We developed a deep-learning framework using a convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict postmenstrual age (PMA) from spontaneous neural activity in EEG recordings of 165 healthy preterm infants (28-38 weeks PMA). The model achieved a mean absolute error of 0.75 ± 0.60 weeks, with 73.9% of prediction errors within one week. To identify key neurophysiological drivers, we systematically manipulated signal components. Results showed that removing low-frequency activity (<4 Hz) significantly degraded performance and disrupting phase-amplitude coupling selectively impaired prediction accuracy before 34 weeks PMA, while high-frequency activity (>12 Hz) had minimal impact. Our results demonstrate that maturation signatures are primarily driven by slow-wave dynamics and their hierarchical coupling with faster oscillations, which are fundamental hallmarks of early neurodevelopment.

papers.title: Expectation-driven gain modulation of preparatory spatial attention.
papers.abstract: The visual system can flexibly adjust attentional deployment to match task demands, but whether observers can proactively modulate the spatial scope of attention based on expectations about upcoming search difficulty remains unclear. According to the zoom lens model, attention can narrow or broaden its spatial extent, with narrower focus enhancing processing efficiency, a mechanism that would benefit target discrimination in crowded displays. We tested whether observers adjust attentional scope when expecting sparse versus dense search arrays by combining spatial cueing with block-wise manipulations of display density expectations. Participants performed a visual search task in which endogenous cues predicted target location, while blocks predominantly contained either sparse (1 target, 3 distractors) or dense (1 target, 7 distractors) displays. We applied inverted encoding models to broadband EEG data to reconstruct spatial channel tuning functions, enabling precise characterization of both the locus and breadth of attentional deployment. Behaviorally, expecting difficult searches selectively improved accuracy at cued locations without costs elsewhere. Consistent with this selective benefit, neural measurements revealed that expectancy enhanced the amplitude of spatially selective responses at the attended location but did not alter tuning width. These findings demonstrate that expectations about search difficulty modulate attention through gain-based signal enhancement rather than adjustments to spatial scope, revealing that preparatory attentional control operates via amplitude modulation within a stable spatial focus. This mechanism complements reactive attentional adjustments and provides an efficient means for the visual system to optimize processing under predictable task demands.

papers.title: Distinct motor preparatory signals correlate with coarse vs fine control of self-paced action timing.
papers.abstract: Making each action at the right time is crucial for motor control. In this study, we investigated how two prominent motor preparatory processes identified in human EEG-beta-band desynchronisation and the readiness potential (RP)-might each differently relate to the time of a simple voluntary action. In our paradigm, participants learned when to act in each block of trials, based on probabilistic trial-by-trial feedback. A reward schedule reinforced a specific optimal time to act in some blocks, but allowed greater variability around the same mean action time in other blocks. We found that contralateral motor beta-band power at the beginning of each trial was higher in trials with slow actions than in those with fast actions. In contrast, contralateral beta-band power reached stereotyped low values at the time of action, regardless of waiting times. Put together, this pattern is consistent with a neural implementation of distance-to-bound for a noisy accumulation process, in which baseline motor activity starts off closer to an action-triggering bound when fast actions are required. In turn, the RP was independent of the mean waiting time before action, but its slope increased when participants developed a precise motor plan. We suggest that beta desynchronisation and the RP track distinct, complementary processes involved in the temporal control of action. While beta-power activity at trial onset is consistent with a strategic adjustment of motor preparation to match the required pace of action, the modulation of the RP by motor plan precision is consistent with a temporally structured input to a ramping preparatory process. Simulations suggest that acting at the right time may involve increasing the strength of the input to this accumulator, which can drive the decision variable to drift towards the decision bound.

papers.title: Age-specific pediatric templates improve EEG source-reconstructed biomarkers in children
papers.abstract: EEG source reconstruction requires an anatomical head model, ideally constructed from individual magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. In developmental studies of children and adolescents, however, MRIs are rarely available. Researchers therefore routinely rely on adult templates, such as the FreeSurfer average (fsaverage), despite substantial anatomical changes throughout development. How much this reliance on adult models biases downstream EEG biomarkers remains unclear. Here, we investigated whether age-specific pediatric templates offer a better alternative to fsaverage for EEG-derived biomarkers in children and adolescents, using individual MRI-based reconstruction as the reference. We analyzed eyes-closed resting-state EEGs from 384 Healthy Brain Network participants aged 5.5 to 17.5 years. For each participant, we tested three anatomical models: their individual MRI, an age-specific pediatric template from a series spanning ages 6-17 at one-year intervals, and the adult fsaverage template. We compared four EEG biomarkers in childhood and adolescence: absolute power, relative power, long-range temporal correlations quantified with detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA), and functional excitation-inhibition (fE/I) ratio. Pediatric templates agreed more closely with individual MRI-based biomarkers in both developmental groups and had fewer parcels with significantly different biomarker values than the adult template, except for absolute power in older adolescents. We conclude that when individual MRI is not available, age-specific pediatric templates match individual MRI-based EEG biomarker values more closely than the adult template across all four biomarkers up to approximately 12 years of age and should be the preferred choice at least up to this age.

Pediatric templates matched individual MRI-based biomarker values more closely than the adult template across power, DFA, and fE/I measures up to about age 12, supporting their use when individual MRI is unavailable.

papers.title: Temporal coupling shapes the effects of prolonged muscle-tendon vibration on sensorimotor EEG activity during motor imagery.
papers.abstract: Motor imagery (MI) recruits sensorimotor networks overlapping those engaged during physical execution and represents a promising rehabilitation tool. While concurrent afferent stimulation enhances MI-related cortical engagement, the effects of prolonged proprioceptive conditioning prior to MI remain unexplored. This study investigated whether prolonged muscle-tendon vibration (MTV) could modulate cortical activity during subsequent MI, indexed by electroencephalographic alpha- and beta-band event-related desynchronization (ERD). Twenty healthy adults performed imagined maximal isometric knee extensions before and after 20-minute suprapatellar MTV (100 Hz) or SHAM vibration (30 Hz with foam interface) in counterbalanced sessions. Cortical engagement was assessed via EEG burst detection over central electrodes (C3, Cz, C4). Maximal force capacity, submaximal force estimation performance, and cortical responses during combined MI and MTV were also evaluated. MTV induced stronger vibratory responses than SHAM, consistent with enhanced proprioceptive afferent activation. Following MTV, voluntary force outcomes showed near-threshold changes consistent with the expected direction, namely reduced maximal force capacity and altered submaximal force calibration, suggesting modified proprioceptive feedback. MI performed after MTV conditioning exhibited reduced alpha- and beta-band ERD compared to SHAM, with greater vibratory-induced responses being associated with a less pronounced post-vibration beta ERD. Conversely, when MI was performed concurrently with MTV following conditioning, alpha-band ERD increased selectively in the MTV session, with no modulation in the beta band. These findings suggest that prolonged proprioceptive conditioning modulates MI-related cortical engagement differently depending on the sensorimotor context in which imagery is performed. Such state-dependent effects may support distinct intervention strategies aimed either at recalibrating maladaptive sensorimotor patterns or at enhancing cortical recruitment in rehabilitation contexts.

papers.title: Participant-Disjoint EEG Decoding of Instructed Respiratory Conditions Using a Deep Spatio-Respiratory Transformer.
papers.abstract: Fine-grained classification of instructed respiratory conditions from non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) remains challenging because of low signal-to-noise ratio and substantial inter-participant variability. This study proposes a Deep Spatio-Respiratory Transformer (DSRT) for EEG-based classification of instructed respiratory conditions. DSRT integrates differential entropy (DE) and normalized power-ratio (NPR) features, squeeze-and-excitation-based feature recalibration, a four-layer feature-token Transformer encoder, and auxiliary nasal/oral pathway supervision. The final task comprised eight respiratory-condition classes. The framework was evaluated using 64-channel EEG from 13 unique participants contributing 21 recording sessions. A fixed-count window-selection strategy was used to equalize the number of retained EEG windows across classes, and model evaluation was performed using participant-disjoint outer folds. Primary architecture comparisons and feature-representation analyses were conducted using participant-level performance summaries. At the participant level, DSRT achieved an Accuracy of 0.7429 ± 0.0492. Compared with EEG Conformer, the strongest matched-input comparison architecture, DSRT improved Accuracy and Macro-F1 by 3.78 and 3.79 percentage points, respectively. Architectural ablation showed the largest performance reduction after removal of the Transformer encoder, while participant-level feature-sensitivity analysis showed that the combined DE-NPR representation outperformed either feature family alone. DSRT contained 1.297 million parameters and achieved a median window-to-prediction latency of 3.825 ms. Duration-matched analysis further identified spatially heterogeneous EEG differences associated with instructed nasal and oral breathing. DSRT provides a participant-disjoint framework for fine-grained classification of EEG patterns associated with instructed respiratory conditions while retaining millisecond-scale inference. The findings support the utility of hybrid spectral representations and feature-token dependency modeling.

papers.title: Mental-Fatigue-Related Changes in EEG Microstate Dynamics and Microstate-Conditioned Phase-Amplitude Coupling.
papers.abstract: Mental fatigue in pilots is a critical risk factor for flight safety. This study aimed to characterize electroencephalographic (EEG) microstate temporal dynamics and microstate-conditioned phase-amplitude coupling across different levels of mental fatigue during a simulated-flight task, and to examine the within-participant associations between these measures. EEG signals were acquired during simulated-flight tasks to analyze neural activity patterns across different mental fatigue levels. The study focused on the temporal parameters of EEG microstates, and the theta-low-beta, theta-high-beta, alpha-low-beta, and alpha-high-beta phase-amplitude couplings (PACs) in the frontal and parietal lobe regions. Linear mixed-effects models were employed to analyze how microstate parameters and PAC metrics varied with mental fatigue levels. Repeated-measures correlations examined within-participant associations between microstate C temporal parameters and PAC under low and high mental fatigue. Compared with the low mental fatigue condition, high mental fatigue was associated with shorter duration, lower occurrence, and lower time coverage of microstate C. Within microstate C, high mental fatigue was associated with higher theta-low-beta PAC in the left parietal and right frontal regions; theta-high-beta PAC in the left frontal, left parietal, and right frontal regions; alpha-low-beta PAC in the bilateral frontal regions; and alpha-high-beta PAC in the right frontal region. Repeated-measures correlations further revealed multiple significant negative within-participant associations between microstate C temporal parameters and microstate C-conditioned PAC under both fatigue conditions. More associations survived FDR correction under high mental fatigue, and most corresponding coefficients were numerically more negative; however, between-condition differences in the correlation coefficients were not formally tested. These findings characterize mental-fatigue-related changes in microstate temporal dynamics and microstate-conditioned PAC, together with exploratory within-participant associations between these measures, and provide new insights into the neural activity patterns associated with mental fatigue.

papers.title: Feedback Valence, Prediction Error, and the Limits of Computational Attribution in Symptom-Related EEG
papers.abstract: Feedback-locked electroencephalography (EEG) responses are often interpreted using model-derived prediction errors (PEs), although signed PE can be strongly coupled to feedback valence in binary-outcome tasks. We revisited a published anxiety-related EEG association using two open probabilistic-learning datasets to examine measurement reliability, predictor separability, and participant-level recovery. In the primary dataset, greater trait anxiety was associated with a larger negative-minus-positive FCz theta response among 46 participants with elevated depressive symptoms after adjustment for depression severity. The association also differed between the sampled depression-symptom groups. The feedback contrast showed useful within-session reliability, but matched delta and P3-minus-N2 analyses did not establish theta specificity. Within participants, feedback valence and signed PE were highly correlated (r = -0.964). Exact-design simulations showed that population-level model discrimination could succeed despite poor recovery of individual neural slopes. Participant-specific learning-model refits recovered overall signed PE more consistently than the within-valence variation needed to distinguish it from feedback valence. An independent dataset reproduced the FCz feedback contrast in untreated and placebo cohorts but lacked trait-anxiety scores. Adding signed PE to valence yielded a small held-out predictive improvement under one reinforcement-learning specification, with limited support across sessions and no comparable support under the dual-rate model or in placebo. Together, these findings support a symptom-related feedback EEG association while constraining its theta-specific and participant-level computational interpretation.

papers.title: Human iEEG recordings during audiovisual speech violations support and extend predictive routing models.
papers.abstract: Rather than constantly reconstructing the world solely through sensory input, predictive processing theories posit that the brain utilizes predictions maintained as internal representations to guide sensory processing. An emerging model, predictive routing, proposes that an interplay between neuronal gamma (40-150 Hz) and alpha-beta (10-30 Hz) rhythms implements a dynamic mechanism for predictive processing. Namely, predictions enhance alpha-beta oscillations that suppress gamma activity during the processing of predicted inputs. While this model is supported by animal studies, its validity has not been fully explored within the human brain. The present study addresses this by leveraging human intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings across superior temporal and prefrontal/premotor areas of seven presurgical epilepsy patients during an audiovisual speech paradigm. We calculated iEEG power in the theta, alpha-beta, and high gamma bands during simple auditory deviance, multisensory integration, and a condition where an incongruent visual cue (lip movements) clashed with an auditory stimulus (a syllable), creating audiovisual incongruence that can elicit the McGurk illusion. Results revealed increased high-gamma and decreased alpha-beta power in the superior temporal cortex in response to auditory deviance and the McGurk condition, while frontal areas, despite reflecting a similar decrease in alpha-beta power, did not present this high gamma prediction error signal. Instead, the theta band revealed a strong prediction error signal in the McGurk condition, consistent with theories on the role of theta in reorganizing cortical networks. These results both support and extend existing predictive routing models for human-specific forms of predictive processing.

papers.title: Structural and EEG Motor Networks Distinguish Level of Motor Impairment After Stroke.
papers.abstract: The objective of this study was to determine how structural and EEG-based functional connectivity jointly distinguish levels of motor impairment after stroke. We estimated patient-specific (1) structural connectivity using MRI-derived lesion models and (2) functional connectivity using source-localized EEG, guided by each patient's structural connectome. Analyses focused on the brainstem and three motor-related cortical regions bilaterally: primary motor cortex (M1), dorsal premotor cortex (PMd), and supplementary motor cortex (SMA). Network analysis metrics (degree centrality, average efficiency, betweenness centrality) were applied to structural and functional data, contrasting motor networks between patients with high (H) and low (L) upper extremity motor function. Structural disconnection of the brainstem from M1 and PMd carried the highest probability of low motor status. All network measures were elevated in the H group compared to the L group across motor-related regions, indicating a globally strengthened motor network organization associated with better motor function. Functional connectivity revealed convergent but distinct patterns. In the delta band (1-3 Hz), ipsilesional motor regions showed stronger connectivity in the H group. In the beta band (14-29 Hz), contralesional motor regions demonstrated enhanced connectivity in H patients, consistent with prior evidence that contralesional motor regions may contribute to motor function after ipsilesional injury. We also introduced a novel metric, motor betweenness centrality, to quantify the role of nonmotor regions in rerouting motor-related communication. Almost all new hubs identified structurally were associated with lower motor status, suggesting less efficient network organization in more impaired patients. Thus, preservation of direct motor pathways supports better motor status, while reliance on alternative, less efficient routes correlates with worse outcomes. By contrast, EEG routing revealed that H patients recruited proximal cortical hubs, while L patients relied on distant, inefficient ones, highlighting functional network organization not evident in the structural analysis. These patterns suggest that more local network organization, rather than more distributed rerouting, is associated with better motor status within the motor system. In summary, multimodal network properties reliably identified key motor ROIs predictive of motor status. This concordance suggests that EEG-based metrics, particularly delta- and beta-band connectivity, are associated with lesion-derived structural disruption and complementary features of motor-network organization. Structural connectivity damage within motor circuits defines the extent of network disruption associated with motor impairment, while EEG functional connectivity provides complementary information about network organization measured at the time of assessment. Together, these measures characterize different aspects of motor network integrity after stroke.

papers.title: Opposing effects of childhood abuse and neglect on neural performance monitoring.
papers.abstract: The dimensional model of adversity proposes that threat (abuse) and deprivation (neglect) exert distinct effects on neurocognitive development. We tested whether these dimensions show opposing associations with neural indices of performance monitoring in a sample of 782 young adults from the CoScience EEG-Personality Project. Participants completed the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire alongside an Eriksen flanker task while electroencephalography was recorded. Performance monitoring was indexed by the error-related negativity and frontal midline theta activity. Consistent with preregistered hypotheses, abuse and neglect showed opposing associations with both neural measures. Higher abuse was associated with enhanced error-related negativity but not theta power, whereas higher neglect was associated with attenuated error-related negativity and reduced theta power. Exploratory analyses indicated that these associations were moderated by sex, with stronger effects observed in males. These findings are consistent with the distinction between threat- and deprivation-related adversity and suggest that different forms of childhood adversity may be linked to variation in neurocognitive processes underlying cognitive control. However, the cross-sectional and retrospective nature of the measures limits causal inference and may introduce reporting biases.

papers.title: Transforming neurophysiological data into measurable stress metric using machine learning-based stress quantification framework for smart factory workers.
papers.abstract: Mental stress is a common issue in demanding occupational setups, such as smart industrial settings, particularly when working with robots, being one of the primary reasons for decreased performance and productivity. Estimating and evaluating stress are critical for worker safety, performance, and overall well-being. A novel integrated framework is proposed in this research for continuous cognitive stress-level estimation that combines neuroimaging (EEG and fNIRS), gaze tracking and machine learning. A factory workers' stress assessment experiment is designed and implemented, which employs physiological, behavioral and subjective measures to assess mental stress from different perspectives. Physiological features extracted from multimodal neuroimaging data are used for training supervised classification and regression models, while gaze, behavioral, and subjective measures provide complementary evaluation of worker stress. To further optimize the pipeline, multiple feature selection algorithms are tested, followed by ensemble learning approaches, and the best model is chosen for continuous stress-level estimation. After implementing the novel stress quantification framework for the factory workers' stress assessment experiment, the ensemble learning approach produced the best results for both regression (RMSE: 10.86) and classification (accuracy: 84.1%) techniques using the STAI score as the target. The behavioral and subjective measures demonstrate the effect of varying process variables (light, noise, task speed, and complexity) during the experiment. Multimodal data, machine learning, and other computational approaches are integrated in this study to estimate continuous cognitive stress levels, utilizing the proposed framework presented in this research, thereby bridging the gap between research and practical application. The proposed multi-domain framework provides a promising solution for monitoring worker well-being in occupational settings.

papers.title: Spectral power and functional connectivity of resting EEG in people exposed to armed conflict and controls.
papers.abstract: Exposure to armed conflict can leave persistent effects on mental health, yet its neurophysiological correlates remain poorly characterized, particularly in populations exposed to prolonged violence outside narrowly defined post traumatic stress disorder samples. Here we examined resting state electroencephalographic activity in 122 Colombian adults, including 74 participants exposed to armed conflict and 48 controls. Eyes closed EEG was analysed for 240 seconds per participant. We quantified absolute and relative spectral power across delta, theta, alpha and beta bands and regional functional connectivity using weighted phase lag index in theta, alpha and beta. Group comparisons were adjusted for age, education, sex and assessment year, with correction across 78 EEG contrasts. Median occipital and global alpha power was lower in exposed participants, although adjusted estimates were close to the null and confidence intervals were broad. Temporal theta relative power was lower in exposed participants at nominal significance; the contrast did not retain statistical significance after Holm correction. No spectral power or regional connectivity contrast met the adjusted significance threshold. Exploratory associations between EEG measures and MoCA performance were modest among participants without scoring flags. These findings characterize resting EEG in a population shaped by prolonged violence and displacement. The confidence intervals leave the magnitude and direction of several group differences uncertain, while the observed alpha and theta patterns identify questions for larger studies integrating more detailed exposure and cognitive measures.

papers.title: Mirror Neural System in Hands Motor Imagery with Pictures and Videos Guidance: An EEG-fNIRS Study.
papers.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) achieved by motor imagery (MI) have been widely accepted as an effective tool in rehabilitative applications. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and electroencephalography (EEG) are two common implementation forms of BCIs, capable of monitoring neuronal potential changes and hemodynamic variations during different tasks. MI and action observation are often employed in therapeutic settings for patients with hemiplegia or other conditions that prevent actual movements. Decoding physiological signals during the imagination process plays a role in facilitating rehabilitation. However, the role of guided motor imagery in the imagination process has not been well studied. In this study, we compared the activation levels of oxygenated hemoglobin, the changes of neural activities' power in terms of time and frequency, and the differences and similarities of neural activations in the cortex area across seven different motor tasks under four conditions: motor execution (ME), MI, picture-guided motor imagery (PGMI) and video-guided motor imagery (VGMI). These findings demonstrate that although guided motor imagery (GMI) does not ease imagination tasks according to participant feedback, GMI reliably recruits mirror neurons during imagination when analyzing fNIRS and EEG signals. The results highlight that GMI has the potential to enrich BCI-based rehabilitation protocols for effectiveness enhancement.

papers.title: Intranasal CBT101 demonstrates favorable safety and neurophysiological evidence of central activity in healthy male volunteers.
papers.abstract: CBT101 is a creatine prodrug under development for disorders driven by impaired neuronal energy homeostasis, with initial development focused on creatine transporter deficiency and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. This first-in-human study aimed to assess the safety and tolerability of single and repeated ascending intranasal doses of CBT101 in healthy male volunteers and explored neurophysiological evidence of central pharmacodynamic activity using quantitative EEG (qEEG) and event-related potentials (ERPs). This was a randomized, double-blind, single-center, placebo-controlled phase 1 trial including single ascending dose (SAD) and multiple ascending dose (MAD) parts. Forty-eight healthy male volunteers were randomized 3:1 to CBT101 or placebo. CBT101 was administered intranasally at 4.2, 8.4, or 12.6 mg in the SAD part and at 4.2, 8.4, or 12.6 mg/day for 14 days in the MAD part. The primary objective was safety and tolerability. Secondary analyses assessed quantitative EEG (qEEG) and event-related potentials (ERPs) as pharmacodynamic evaluations. No serious or severe treatment-emergent adverse events occurred, no dose-limiting toxicity was observed, and no clinically relevant safety findings were reported. As expected, plasma CBT101 concentrations were below the limit of quantification in all analyzed samples. qEEG analyses identified an acute post-dose increase in relative beta activity after single dosing. After repeated dosing, the qEEG profile evolved toward a more sustained pattern characterized by beta-1 modulation and early gamma-band changes. ERP/P300 analyses showed a transient decrease in P300 latency, with no statistically significant change in P300 amplitude. Intranasal CBT101 was safe and well tolerated across the evaluated SAD and MAD dose ranges in healthy male volunteers. Convergent qEEG and ERP findings provided early neurophysiological evidence of central pharmacodynamic engagement. These findings support continued clinical development of CBT101 for disorders associated with impaired neuronal energy homeostasis. ClinicalTrials.gov, identifier: NCT07050316.

papers.title: Generative-augmented multimodal neuroaffective decoding for product evaluation: toward neurofeedback-driven human-in-the-loop co-design.
papers.abstract: Kansei engineering traditionally relies on self-reported evaluations of product impressions, which are susceptible to contextual influences, recall bias, and assessment timing. Multimodal psychophysiological measurements offer complementary insights into affective responses, but integrating heterogeneous signals with limited sample sizes remains challenging. This study proposes Generative-Augmented Multimodal Affective Fusion (GAMAF) to predict perceived attractiveness, innovativeness, and friendliness in product evaluation. GAMAF integrates feature-space conditional Wasserstein generative adversarial learning with gradient penalty (cWGAN-GP), cross-modal attention, graph-based interactions, and adaptive modality weighting. Fifty participants evaluated three automobile cockpit designs, yielding 150 participant-stimulus trials after multimodal quality control. Electroencephalography (EEG), eye tracking (ET), and peripheral physiological signals were integrated and evaluated using nested participant-wise cross-validation. GAMAF achieved mean outer-fold R² values of 0.810, 0.850, and 0.840 for attractiveness, innovativeness, and friendliness, respectively, each with a standard deviation of 0.016. These values exceeded those of the Multimodal Transformer baseline (0.75, 0.78, and 0.76, respectively). Across the three targets, GAMAF reduced aggregate mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) by approximately 29.6% and 29.7%, respectively. Ablation analyses supported the integrated architecture, while adaptive modality weights revealed target-dependent patterns. GAMAF demonstrates the potential of generative-augmented multimodal fusion for decoding Kansei-related product impressions. However, performance comparisons remain descriptive because baseline variability and participant-level uncertainty were not quantified. Further validation on unseen product designs and closed-loop design optimization is needed to establish its generalizability and practical utility.

papers.title: Scalable hardware and software for high-density, multi-regional electrophysiology in non-human primates.
papers.abstract: Understanding how distributed neural circuits generate complex behaviors requires long-duration recordings from populations of individual neurons across multiple brain regions. High-density Neuropixels probes have revolutionized rodent systems neuroscience. Extending these capabilities to non-human primates (NHPs) for chronic, multi-regional recordings requires compact, implantable microdrive hardware and reliable automated spike-sorting software. NHPs provide access to complex and flexible behaviors that are difficult to study in other model systems. Extending the Neuropixels revolution to NHPs therefore depends on integrating hardware and software for long-duration, multi-regional recordings. Here, we present a scalable hardware-software platform co-designed for high-density neural data acquisition and reliable single-unit identification in NHPs. The Multi-regional Implantable NeuroDrive (MIND) is a lightweight, implantable microdrive that provides stable recordings from multiple independently positioned Neuropixels probes and is designed to support chronic, ambulatory, head-free recordings. We paired MIND with UnitAssay, an automated post-sorting curation framework that identifies and curates characteristic spike-sorting errors with minimal computational cost. Together, MIND and UnitAssay provide an integrated platform for implanted, multi-regional recordings in NHPs performing complex and naturalistic behaviors. We tested MIND and UnitAssay across parietal, prefrontal, and motor cortices in rhesus macaques performing reaching and eye-movement tasks. MIND enabled stable multi-probe recordings across cortical regions and durations. UnitAssay enabled automated curation of large-scale spike-sorting output and improved reliable single-unit identification relative to Kilosort 4 labels and standard SpikeInterface quality control. Together, MIND and UnitAssay provide a scalable solution for high-density, multi-regional, long-duration electrophysiology in NHPs.

papers.title: Resting-State EEG Spectral Power in Young Adults With Generalized Anxiety Disorder and Self-Reported Habitual Short Sleep: A Case-Control Study.
papers.abstract: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and insufficient sleep frequently co-occur during early adulthood, yet resting-state electroencephalographic (EEG) evidence in this population remains limited. The present study aimed to characterize resting-state EEG spectral power in young adults with GAD who also reported habitual short sleep, compared with healthy controls. This exploratory case-control study included 56 university students: 28 participants with GAD and self-reported habitual short sleep and 28 healthy controls. Resting-state EEG spectral power was quantified in the delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands. We retained unadjusted group comparisons for description and fitted age- and sex-adjusted linear models for the primary inferential interpretation. Channel-wise models likewise included group, age, and sex, with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction across the 30 channels within each frequency band. After adjustment for age and sex, group coefficients remained positive for delta (2.51, 95% CI: 0.20 to 4.82), theta (2.52, 95% CI: 0.29 to 4.74), alpha (2.46, 95% CI: -0.12 to 5.03), and beta power (2.14, 95% CI: 0.13 to 4.15), but none met the FDR threshold (adjusted FDR p = 0.0501, 0.0501, 0.0608, and 0.0501, respectively). In unadjusted analyses, delta, theta, and beta differences survived FDR correction (FDR p = 0.0480 for each), whereas alpha did not (FDR p = 0.0553). In adjusted channel-wise analyses, 26 channel-by-band comparisons across 15 channels survived within-band FDR correction; all occurred in delta or theta and were concentrated over posterior and centroparietal electrodes. Whole-scalp estimates were directionally higher in the GAD plus habitual short-sleep group, but no age- and sex-adjusted frequency-band comparison survived FDR correction. Adjusted exploratory channel-wise findings indicated a posterior and centroparietal concentration in delta and theta power. These estimates remain preliminary and do not permit attribution to GAD, habitual short sleep, or their interaction.

papers.title: Behavioral, biochemical, histological, and electrophysiological changes following intracerebral injection of bone marrow stem cell-derived exosomes in male rat models of Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Recently, researchers have been exploring how exosomes can help treat neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), has attracted considerable attention. This study aimed to investigate behavioral, biochemical, histological, and electrophysiological changes following the administration of bone marrow stem cell-derived exosomes (Exo-BMSCs) in AD model rats. Animals were divided into control, Lesion (Lesion, Lesion + saline), and treatment (Lesion + BMSCs, Lesion + Exo-BMSCs) groups. BMSCs were extracted from the bone marrow of newborn rats. Exosomes were extracted from the BMSCs culture medium using a chemical kit. Saline, BMSCs, and Exo-BMSCs were injected bilaterally into the nucleus of Meynert (NBM) one week after electrical lesion. 28 days after injection, behavioral, electrophysiological, and histological changes, as well as ACh and BDNF expression levels in the hippocampus, were evaluated. Electrical lesion of the NBM caused a significant decrease in passive avoidance memory retrieval, a significant decrease in ACh and BDNF levels, changes in EEG wave frequencies in the hippocampus, and histological changes in the NBM, similar to those observed in AD. On the other hand, injection of BMSCs and Exo-BMSCs into the NBM significantly improved passive avoidance memory, an increase in BDNF levels, an increase in power of gamma waves, and improved histological changes compared to the Lesion groups. The increase in power of gamma waves was significant only in the Exo-BMSC-treated group. Injection of BMSCs and Exo-BMSCs into the NBM can significantly improve disease symptoms. This improvement was more pronounced in the Exo-BMSCs-treated group. The concurrent increase in BDNF suggests that this neurotrophin contributes to the observed effects.

papers.title: Different modes of stimulation at the Neiguan acupoint (PC6) regulate different EEG microstates under VR immersion conditions.
papers.abstract: Acupuncture at the Neiguan acupoint (PC6) alleviates postoperative and chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Nevertheless, the central regulatory effects of PC6 stimulation on virtual reality motion sickness (VRMS), a form of physiological vertigo triggered by visual-vestibular sensory conflict, and the corresponding alterations in electroencephalogram (EEG) microstate characteristics remain unclear. Using EEG microstate analysis as the primary approach, this study investigated the effects of different PC6 stimulation modalities on dynamic brain functional changes during VRMS, aiming to further elucidate the potential neural mechanisms underlying acupoint stimulation in VRMS. Participants were recruited based on their Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire scores, with a cut-off value of ≥34 used as the inclusion criterion. A total of 200 healthy participants were enrolled and randomly assigned to four equal groups (n = 50 per group): control (32 °C), 40 °C, 44 °C, and 2-Hz transcutaneous electrical acupoint stimulation (TEAS). The experimental protocol consisted of three phases: baseline, active stimulation, and post-stimulation. All participants received a 40-min stimulation targeting the right PC6 acupoint. EEG data were continuously recorded throughout the experiment. Microstate analysis revealed that during the stimulation phase, the 2-Hz TEAS group exhibited significantly increased duration, occurrence, and coverage of microstate D compared with the control group, whereas the 40 °C group affected only the duration of microstate D. During the post-stimulation phase, compared with the control group, the 44 °C group showed a decreased duration of microstate A and significantly increased duration and coverage of microstate B, while the 2-Hz TEAS group continued to exhibit sustained effects on the duration of microstate D. The neuroelectrophysiological signatures of stimulation at PC6 in modulating VRMS are predominantly reflected in the dynamic changes of microstates A, B, and D. Thermal stimulation and low-frequency electrical stimulation engage distinct central modulatory pathways, providing a neuroelectrophysiological basis for optimizing stimulation parameters for in future studies on VRMS.

Findings indicate that different PC6 stimulation modes modulate VR motion sickness through partially distinct central pathways reflected in microstates A, B, and D.

papers.title: Clinical characteristics, semiology, and comorbidity patterns in non-epileptic seizures (NES): a retrospective comparative study.
papers.abstract: Non-epileptic seizures (NES) are paroxysmal events resembling epileptic seizures but not explained by ictal activity. Differential diagnosis may be challenging, particularly because NES and epilepsy can coexist. We aimed to characterize the demographic, clinical, semiological, psychiatric, and instrumental profile of patients with NES, compare patients with NES only with patients with NES epilepsy-only, and assess the robustness of the main associations through sensitivity analyses. We conducted a retrospective observational comparative study using a clinical database from our Neurology Unit (2022-2025) including 38 patients with NES and 23 patients with epilepsy without NES. A total of 18 NES patients had comorbid epilepsy; therefore, the primary comparison included mutually exclusive groups: NES-only (n = 20) and epilepsy-only (n = 23). All NES patients were retained for descriptive analyses. Between-group comparisons used exact or non-parametric tests with Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate (BH-FDR) correction. Sensitivity analyses restricted NES-only patients to those with database-recorded video-EEG confirmation and used Firth penalized logistic regression adjusted for age and sex. Among 38 patients with NES, 94.7% had documented psychological/psychiatric comorbidity, mainly anxiety (50.0%) and depression (28.9%). Positive motor phenomena were documented in 73.7%, neurological examination inconsistency/incongruity in 85.7% of evaluable patients, and video-EEG confirmation in 73.7%. Psychological/psychiatric comorbidity was significantly more frequent in NES-only than epilepsy-only patients (90.0% vs. 13.0%; exact OR 50.40, 95% CI 7.29-670.28; BH-FDR p < 0.001), as was anxiety (45.0% vs. 4.3%; BH-FDR p = 0.014). Broad seizure-semiology domains were not significantly different after multiplicity correction. Among imaged patients, abnormal MRI findings were more frequent in epilepsy-only patients (12/18 vs. 0/10; BH-FDR p = 0.006), although MRI ascertainment differed between groups. The psychiatric-comorbidity association persisted in sensitivity analyses. NES showed substantial clinical heterogeneity and frequently coexisted with epilepsy. Psychological/psychiatric comorbidity was markedly more frequent in NES-only than epilepsy-only patients and remained robust in sensitivity analyses, although differential ascertainment limits interpretation. Broad seizure manifestations alone did not distinguish the groups after multiplicity correction. Instrumental findings should be considered descriptive rather than NES biomarkers. These findings support explicit stratification for comorbid epilepsy and standardized prospective assessment of psychiatric and semiological features.

papers.title: Decoding and Characterizing the Intracranial Representation of Semantic Information
papers.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have achieved impressive performance by decoding motor and articulatory signals associated with speech production. However, considerably less is known about whether higher-level semantic representations can be decoded from human cortical activity. Demonstrating semantic decoding would advance both our understanding of language organization and the development of BCIs that rely on conceptual rather than purely articulatory information. We recorded intracranial neural activity from patients undergoing stereotactic electroencephalography (sEEG) for clinical epilepsy monitoring while they performed language tasks requiring semantic processing. High-gamma power was extracted from local field potentials and used to generate trial-level features for supervised machine-learning classification. Classification performance was evaluated using cross-validation. Semantic category information was decoded significantly above chance, with mean classification accuracy reaching 29.8% across 15 semantic categories (chance = 6.7%). These findings demonstrate that high-gamma activity contains information about conceptual category membership that can be extracted on individual trials. These results provide evidence that semantic information is accessible from intracranial population recordings and support the feasibility of semantic decoding as a complementary direction for future language BCIs. Beyond neuroprosthetic applications, this work contributes to understanding how conceptual knowledge is represented in the distributed human language network.

papers.title: Integrating uncertainty and practice variability for epilepsy prognostication after intracranial EEG: A meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) practices and diagnostic testing vary among institutions, limiting standardization and optimization of surgical outcomes. This study estimates resection rates and surgical outcome effect sizes after iEEG and develops individual patient-level data (IPD) models using the missing-indicator method to approximate real-world clinical uncertainties and practice variability in iEEG and surgical decision-making. Databases were queried for studies reporting ≥12-month outcomes after epilepsy surgery in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) who underwent iEEG. Random-effects meta-analysis estimated pooled outcome proportions. IPD analysis was performed using multivariable generalized linear regression and logistic regression models with cross-validation and calibration assessment. Missing values for key predictors were retained as a "not specified" category to evaluate the impact of incorporating uncertainty in common clinical data on outcome prediction. Primary outcomes were seizure freedom (Engel class IA or International League Against Epilepsy [ILAE] 1) and favorable seizure outcomes (Engel I or ILAE 1-2). Of 4975 studies identified, 115 met the inclusion criteria. The pooled frequency of patients undergoing resection after iEEG was 67% (95% confidence interval [CI] 60%-74%), 52% achieved seizure freedom (95% CI 48%-56%), and 58% achieved a favorable outcome (95% CI 54%-62%). IPD analysis included 1305 patients from 29 studies and identified a lesional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI; odds ratio [OR] 1.94, CI 1.48-2.55, p < .0001) and a cortical malformation (OR 1.47, CI 1.08-2.00, p = .01) as independent predictors of a favorable outcome, whereas iEEG implantation strategy (bilateral implantation OR .61, 95% CI .42-.89, p = .01) was an independent predictor of a less favorable outcome. About two-thirds of patients undergoing iEEG proceeded to resection, and about half achieved seizure freedom. Multivariable models incorporating clinical uncertainty and practice variability were well calibrated. However, modest discrimination suggests that routinely available clinical variables alone have limited ability to predict individual surgical outcomes. More standardized and granular clinical and practice-related data may improve individualized prognostication after iEEG.

papers.title: Advancing Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for Depression: Novel Protocols, Precision Targeting, and Future Directions.
papers.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) remains a significant global health challenge, with substantial limitations inherent in current pharmacotherapeutic and psychotherapeutic approaches. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) has emerged as a safe, effective, and non-invasive neuromodulation therapy, particularly for treatment-resistant depression (TRD). However, conventional rTMS is limited by long treatment duration and variable interindividual efficacy. This expert opinion examines recent advances in rTMS optimization strategies aimed at overcoming these limitations. Key areas of progress include the development of novel stimulation protocols such as theta-burst stimulation (TBS); accelerated regimens and priming TMS; the use of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-guided TMS; and the integration of closed-loop systems using real-time electroencephalography (EEG) or functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) feedback. Additionally, technological innovations, including robot-assisted TMS and wearable devices, promise to enhance targeting accuracy and treatment accessibility. Despite these developments, significant challenges impede clinical translation, including the high cost of personalized protocols, insufficient standardization and validation of novel approaches, and technical barriers to closed-loop implementation. Future efforts should focus on cost reduction, large-scale randomized controlled trials, biomarker development, and device portability. Ultimately, optimized rTMS shows significant potential to become a more efficient, precise, and accessible cornerstone of depression therapy.

papers.title: Restorative streetscapes in high-density urban tourism: environmental archetypes, visual attention, and psychophysiological responses.
papers.abstract: In high-density tourist districts, visitors are continuously exposed to the visual environments of surrounding streets, forecourts, and small public spaces before reaching an attraction, and these transitional spaces may influence short-term restorative states. Existing research has typically examined urban-scale streetscape characteristics and human responses under experimental conditions separately, with limited provision of a reproducible procedure for selecting experimental stimuli from large environmental samples. Taking the high-density urban core around Hong Kong's Victoria Harbour as a case study, this study identified 66 tourism-related sites and acquired four fixed-direction streetscape images for each site, yielding 264 images in total. A 66 × 11 objective environmental matrix was constructed from five GIS-based environmental indicators and six streetscape-image proxy indicators. Principal component analysis (PCA) summarized the dominant environmental gradients, and k = 6 K-means was retained as a pragmatic six-group sampling solution aligned with the pre-specified six-scene experimental capacity rather than as a uniquely optimal or stable urban typology. Forty-six of 48 registered adults contributed 108 focal-scene exposures. After BH-FDR correction, significant differences among the six scenes were observed in perceived restorativeness, the proportion of fixations on natural areas of interest (AOIs), gaze entropy, changes in EEG alpha-minus-theta, mean EDA skin conductance level (SCL), and HRV RMSSD, whereas sustained-attention accuracy showed no significant scene effect. Oil Street Art Space exhibited the highest perceived restorativeness (5.69/7), the highest proportion of fixations on natural AOIs (51.4%), and the largest increases in EEG (+2.68) and HRV RMSSD (+11.37 ms), while Western Market showed the lowest restorativeness (4.17/7), the lowest natural-AOI fixation share (31.2%), and the smallest EEG increase (+1.93). Sensitivity analyses showed no evidence of scene-by-order interaction for perceived restorativeness, natural-AOI fixation, gaze entropy, or SART accuracy, but EEG, EDA, and HRV were more order-sensitive; the principal subjective, attentional, EEG, and HRV contrasts remained evident when analysis was restricted to each participant's earliest focal-scene exposure. These findings therefore support scene-configuration contrasts under short-term static visual exposure. Building on the environmental structure of the 66 sites and the multimodal responses to the six experimental scenes, the study further proposes an archetype-calibrated framework for mapping restorative potential in high-density tourist streetscapes, providing a spatial basis for identifying restorative opportunity nodes and priority intervention areas.

papers.title: Yield of epileptiform abnormalities and predictors on routine electroencephalography in a neurology facility in Ghana.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is an essential neurodiagnostic tool for the evaluation of epilepsy and other neurological disorders. However, evidence on the yield of epileptiform abnormalities of routine EEG and its predictors in sub-Saharan Africa remains limited. To determine the yield of epileptiform abnormalities of routine EEG and identify factors associated with epileptiform discharges in a Ghanaian tertiary referral centre. This study included 124 patients who underwent routine outpatient EEG between October 2023 and January 2026. Demographic, clinical, medication, and EEG characteristics were collected using a standardized data extraction form. The primary outcome was the presence of epileptiform discharges. Associations between patient characteristics and epileptiform activity were assessed using Chi-square and Fisher's exact tests. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify independent predictors, with results reported as adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The mean age of participants was 29.4 ± 19.7 years, and 55.6% were male. Epileptiform discharges were identified in 72 patients, yielding an overall epileptiform abnormality of 58.1%. Generalized epilepsy accounted for 83.3% of epileptiform abnormalities. The highest yield was observed among children aged 0-5 years (83.3%) and adults aged ≥ 60 years (75.0%). On bivariate analysis, generalized slowing (90.9%, p = 0.025) and focal slowing (100.0%, p < 0.001) were significantly associated with epileptiform discharges. In multivariable analysis, abnormal EEG background activity remained the only independent predictor of epileptiform discharges (aOR = 23.47, 95% CI: 2.95-186.86, p = 0.003). Routine EEG demonstrated a high yield of epileptiform abnormalities in this Ghanaian tertiary centre. Abnormal EEG background activity was a strong independent predictor of epileptiform discharges, highlighting the importance of careful background assessment during EEG interpretation and supporting the continued use of routine EEG in epilepsy evaluation.

papers.title: Impairment of ictal consciousness and psychosis in drug-resistant focal epilepsy: A retrospective clinical cohort study.
papers.abstract: Psychoses of epilepsy (POE) affect up to 13% of patients with focal epilepsy. Whereas interictal risk factors are well documented, ictal correlates of POE remain poorly characterized. We hypothesized that an impairment of ictal consciousness on the Consciousness Seizure Scale (CSS), would be associated with POE. We assessed the association between ictal clinical features and POE compared to non-POE in adults with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. We retrospectively analyzed a presurgical cohort of adults with drug-resistant focal epilepsy monitored by video-electroencephalography (EEG) or stereo-EEG. For each patient, all seizures with an examination allowing the completion of CSS score were included. POE were identified through standardized psychiatric interviews. Association between ictal features, primarily CSS score, and POE was tested using generalized estimating equations (GEE). Among 232 included seizures (25 from POE group, 207 from non-POE group), the probability of POE varied nonlinearly with ictal consciousness; it peaked at intermediate CSS scores (GEE, OR = 4.31, p = .006). This effect remained after adjustment for duration of both epilepsy (OR=1.06, p = .005) and seizure (OR=1.20, p = .013). Intraclass correlation of CSS was .76 (95%CI, .65-.85), reflecting a low within-patient variance. An older age, more severe depressive and anxiety symptoms were also associated with POE. POE were associated with intermediate impairment of ictal consciousness, suggesting that partial disruption of awareness may favor the emergence of psychotic symptoms. The high level of intrapatient stability for CSS, mostly estimated from non-POE, suggests that CSS could be constant across seizures. This raises the possibility that POE risk could stem from the way consciousness is altered during seizures.
